title: 1 Chronicles 2:42–55
context: The chapter ends with further descendants of Caleb, towns and families in Judah, and a closing notice about families of scribes at Jabez and about Kenites from Hammath, father of the house of Rechab. “father of” a place, as in Ziph, Hebron, Bethlehem, or Kiriath Jearim, likely marks a clan ancestor or founder associated with that town; the exact force of the phrase, and the precise identification of each site, should be left modest where the list itself does not explain it. Caleb here is called the brother of Jerahmeel, which ties this block to Hezron’s sons in 2:9 and 2:18–24, but the chapter has already used Caleb in more than one connection, and the relationship of these notices should not be forced into a single reconstructed family tree. Achsah is named as Caleb’s daughter, a name also borne by the daughter of Caleb in Joshua 15 and Judges 1; that parallel may be noted, without requiring this verse to retell those stories. Jabez in 2:55 is the place where certain families of scribes lived; the man Jabez of chapter 4 is not in this unit and should not be imported. The Kenites and the house of Rechab are named at the close, a brief link to groups already known from the earlier history, not a full account of them. Both traditions read the unit as the Chronicler settling more of Judah’s clans and towns around the line already traced to David, still inside Israel’s families.

verses.text: The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel were Mesha his firstborn, who was the father of Ziph, and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes:
Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel has a firstborn, Mesha, father of Ziph, and there are sons of Mareshah, father of Hebron. The phrase “father of” a town should be taken cautiously, as clan-head or ancestor associated with the place, not as a guarantee of one later site. This Caleb is called Jerahmeel’s brother, which looks back to Hezron’s sons.

Arminian readers take the names as a real Judahite branch, without mapping every town as if the verse were a survey.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hedge the place-names and the relation of this Caleb to earlier Calebs in the chapter. The list is still family history, not a puzzle to be solved at all costs.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema.” Hebron here follows “father of Hebron” in the previous verse, and the four names may be clans rather than only individuals; the verse itself simply calls them sons. Korah in this list is not identified as the Korah of the wilderness revolt.

Arminian readers keep the four names as the record gives them, without borrowing another Korah’s story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse those identifications. The sons of Hebron are named, and the genealogy continues through Shema and Rekem in the next verse.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: Shema became the father of Raham, the father of Jorkeam; and Rekem became the father of Shammai.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shema becomes the father of Raham, father of Jorkeam; Rekem becomes the father of Shammai. Two short descents run on from the sons just named. Jorkeam is not otherwise explained, and should not be given a certain site without evidence the verse does not supply.

Arminian readers take the links as historical notes in Caleb’s wider house, unallegorized.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Jorkeam and Shammai as the text states them, further names in the Judahite register.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: The son of Shammai was Maon; and Maon was the father of Beth Zur.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The son of Shammai was Maon; and Maon was the father of Beth Zur.” Again a person is called father of a place. Beth Zur is a known Judahite name in other books; the identification of this Maon with a particular later town or man should still remain modest.

Arminian readers hear a clan connection to Beth Zur, stated in the genealogy’s own formula, not a full civic history.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same caution. Maon is the father of Beth Zur in this list, a family-and-place notice rather than a narrative.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: Ephah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran became the father of Gazez.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ephah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran became the father of Gazez. The repeated Gazez may be two men of the same name, or another use of the formula; the text does not explain, and a solution should not be invented.

Arminian readers let the concubine and her sons stand as a household record, including the difficult second Gazez, without forcing a tidy scheme.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to fix what the verse leaves compact. Ephah’s sons are named, and Haran is called the father of Gazez.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jothan, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jothan, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.” Jahdai has not been introduced, and the list does not say how he relates to the Caleb material around him. That gap should be left as a gap.

Arminian readers will not invent a missing father-line in order to make the register perfectly smooth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave Jahdai’s connection unstated, as the Chronicler leaves it. Six sons are named, and that is what the verse gives.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: Maacah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Maacah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah.” A second concubine of Caleb is named, with two sons, and the next verse will continue her children.

Arminian readers take Maacah and her sons as further family facts in this Caleb section, not as a moral illustration or a type.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same plain birth notice. The register is still recording Caleb’s household through more than one woman.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: She bore also Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbena and the father of Gibea; and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah.
verses.arminianNotes:
She also bore Shaaph, father of Madmannah, and Sheva, father of Machbena and of Gibea; “and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah.” Achsah is also the name of Caleb’s daughter in Joshua 15 and Judges 1. The parallel may be named; this verse does not retell those stories, and the identification, though commonly made, should not be treated as a new narrative here.

Arminian readers keep Achsah as the daughter named in this list, with the earlier books in view but not imported in full.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also point to Joshua 15 and Judges 1 without turning this genealogical close into those scenes. Place-names attached to Shaaph and Sheva remain modestly identified.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: These were the sons of Caleb, the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath Jearim,
verses.arminianNotes:
“These were the sons of Caleb, the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath Jearim,” The heading seems to start a new Caleb-and-Hur grouping, after Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel. The relationship of these Calebs should not be forced into one reconstructed tree. Kiriath Jearim is a known town; “father of” still needs a modest reading.

Arminian readers take the heading as the Chronicler’s own, and they do not flatten every Caleb into a single man.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave the arrangement as a possible second block in the Caleb material, with Shobal tied to Kiriath Jearim.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: Salma the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth Gader.
verses.arminianNotes:
The heading continues: “Salma the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth Gader.” Bethlehem is here attached to Salma as “father of” the town. This Salma is not automatically the Salma of 2:11 in the Davidic line, though the names match; the text does not say they are the same man.

Arminian readers can note the shared name and still keep this Salma in his present list, the recorded ancestor associated with Bethlehem in this verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse a required merger of the two Salmas. Bethlehem’s attachment here is genealogical and local, not a cue for typology.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: Shobal the father of Kiriath Jearim had sons: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shobal, father of Kiriath Jearim, had sons: “Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth.” The second phrase looks like a clan half rather than a single personal name; the wording is compact, and a precise census should not be invented from it.

Arminian readers leave “half of the Menuhoth” as the text’s own grouping, a family division rather than a riddle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to over-specify the Menuhoth. Shobal’s sons are named in this brief form, and the next verse will list families of Kiriath Jearim.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: The families of Kiriath Jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from them came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites.
verses.arminianNotes:
The families of Kiriath Jearim are the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from them came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites. The verse is a clan list tied to a town, not a story. Zorah and Eshtaol are familiar names in Judah’s story; identifications should still be modest and not pressed into a full map.

Arminian readers take the families as real Judahite groups recorded by the Chronicler.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same town-and-clan register. From Kiriath Jearim’s families come the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites, as the list says.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth Beth Joab, and half of the Manahathites, the Zorites.
verses.arminianNotes:
Salma’s “sons” include Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth Beth Joab, half of the Manahathites, and the Zorites. Place-names and clan-names stand together in one formula, a further sign that “sons” can mark groups as well as individuals in this section.

Arminian readers will not force each item into a single kind of name. The Chronicler is describing Salma’s associated people and towns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let the mixed list stand. Bethlehem appears again, now among other groups tied to Salma, still without a typological reading.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.

verses.text: The families of scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The families of scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.” Jabez here is the place where these scribal families lived. The man Jabez of chapter 4 is not in this unit and should not be read back into the verse. The Kenites and the house of Rechab are named as the close of the chapter, a brief link to groups known from the earlier history, not a full account of them.

Arminian readers keep the scribes, the place, and the Kenite notice as a historical close, unallegorized.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to import the later Jabez narrative or to expand the house of Rechab beyond this line. The chapter ends with Judah’s families, including these scribes at Jabez, still around the line already traced to David.

Both traditions keep the close of the chapter as Judahite family and town history, without allegory and without certain identifications of every site or every Caleb.
